title: Reconstitution: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio
description: Class 12 Accountancy: reconstitution of a partnership on a change in profit-sharing ratio — sacrificing and gaining ratio, treatment of goodwill and accumulated reserves, and revaluation of assets and liabilities.

topics.title: Sacrificing and Gaining Ratio
topics.concept:
A partnership is reconstituted whenever the existing partners change their mutual rights — the simplest case being a change in the profit-sharing ratio (PSR) among the same partners. When the ratio changes, one or more partners gain a share and others sacrifice a share. Identifying who gains and who sacrifices is the first and most important step.

  • Sacrificing Ratio = Old Share − New Share (when positive, the partner has sacrificed).
  • Gaining Ratio = New Share − Old Share (when positive, the partner has gained).

Worked example. A and B share profits 3:2 and decide to share equally (1:1) in future.

  • A: old 3/5, new 1/2 → 3/5 − 1/2 = 6/10 − 5/10 = 1/10 sacrifice.
  • B: old 2/5, new 1/2 → 1/2 − 2/5 = 5/10 − 4/10 = 1/10 gain.

So A sacrifices 1/10 of the profits to B, who gains 1/10. The partner who gains must compensate the partner who sacrifices — mainly for goodwill, covered next. A handy check: the total sacrifice always equals the total gain. Getting the sacrificing/gaining ratio right is essential, because the goodwill adjustment is shared in exactly this ratio.

examples.problem: Example 1: Write the formulas for sacrificing and gaining ratio.
examples.solution:
Old vs new.

  • Sacrificing ratio = Old share − New share.
  • Gaining ratio = New share − Old share.
examples.answer: Sacrificing ratio = Old − New; Gaining ratio = New − Old.

examples.problem: Example 2: X and Y share 3:1 and change to 2:1. Find each partner's sacrifice or gain.
Example 3: When the ratio changes, who compensates whom?
examples.solution:
Gainer pays sacrificer.

  • The gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner (mainly for goodwill).
examples.answer: The gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner (for the share of goodwill given up).

recap:
• Reconstitution: any change in partners' mutual rights; here a change in PSR.
  • Sacrificing ratio = Old − New; Gaining ratio = New − Old. Total sacrifice = total gain.
  • The gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner, mainly for goodwill.

quiz.explanation: Sacrificing ratio = Old share − New share.

quiz.q: On a change in PSR, the gaining partner must:
quiz.explanation: The gainer compensates the sacrificer for goodwill given up.

topics.title: Treatment of Goodwill and Reserves
topics.concept:
When the ratio changes, the goodwill already built up belongs to the old partners in the old ratio. The partner who now gains a share is effectively buying part of that goodwill from the partner who sacrifices. So an adjustment entry is passed, without raising a goodwill account (AS-26 bars self-generated goodwill in the books):

Gaining Partner's Capital A/c  Dr
   To Sacrificing Partner's Capital A/c

The amount = firm's goodwill × the share gained/sacrificed. For example, if goodwill is valued at Rs 60,000 and B gains 1/10 from A, then B's capital is debited and A's capital credited with 60,000 × 1/10 = Rs 6,000.

Next, any accumulated profits, reserves and losses (general reserve, profit & loss balance, workmen compensation reserve, etc.) standing in the balance sheet also belong to the old partners in the old ratio. So they are distributed to the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio before the new ratio takes effect:

  • Reserves and accumulated profits → credited to old partners in the old ratio.
  • Accumulated losses (e.g. a debit P&L balance) → debited to old partners in the old ratio.

The principle behind both adjustments is the same and worth memorising: everything earned or built up before the change belongs to the partners in the OLD ratio. Only future profits will be shared in the new ratio.

examples.problem: Example 1: Goodwill is Rs 50,000. B gains 1/5 from A. Pass the goodwill adjustment entry.
examples.solution:
Gainer pays sacrificer.

  • Amount = 50,000 × 1/5 = 10,000.
  • B's Capital A/c Dr 10,000; To A's Capital A/c 10,000.
examples.answer: B's Capital A/c Dr 10,000; To A's Capital A/c 10,000.

examples.problem: Example 2: A general reserve of Rs 30,000 exists when A and B (old ratio 3:2) change their ratio. How is it distributed?
examples.solution:
Old ratio.

  • It belongs to old partners in the old ratio 3:2.
  • A: 18,000; B: 12,000 (credited to their capitals).
examples.answer: Credited to A and B in the old ratio 3:2 — A Rs 18,000, B Rs 12,000.

examples.problem: Example 3: Why is goodwill not raised in the books on a change in ratio?
examples.solution:
AS-26.

  • AS-26 forbids recording self-generated goodwill.
  • So only an adjustment entry between capitals is passed.
examples.answer: Because AS-26 does not allow self-generated goodwill to be recorded; only a capital-to-capital adjustment is made.

recap:
• Goodwill adjustment: Gaining partner's Capital Dr / To Sacrificing partner's Capital (goodwill × share); no goodwill account raised (AS-26).
  • Reserves & accumulated profits/losses are distributed to old partners in the old ratio.
  • Principle: everything built up before the change belongs to the old ratio.

quiz.q: On a change in PSR, accumulated reserves are distributed in the:
quiz.explanation: They belong to old partners in the old ratio.

quiz.q: The goodwill adjustment entry debits the:
quiz.explanation: The gaining partner's capital is debited; the sacrificer's is credited.

topics.title: Revaluation of Assets and Liabilities
topics.concept:
On reconstitution, the assets and liabilities may not be at their true current values. Any resulting profit or loss belongs to the old partners (it arose under the old arrangement), so we revalue them through a Revaluation Account (also called the Profit & Loss Adjustment Account).

The rules for the Revaluation Account:

  • An increase in an asset or a decrease in a liability is a gain → credited to Revaluation.
  • A decrease in an asset or an increase in a liability is a loss → debited to Revaluation.
  • Any unrecorded asset brought in is a gain (credit); any unrecorded liability is a loss (debit).
Dr — Revaluation Account — Cr 
To decrease in assetsBy increase in assets
To increase in liabilitiesBy decrease in liabilities
To unrecorded liabilitiesBy unrecorded assets
To profit transferred to partners (old ratio)or By loss transferred to partners (old ratio)

The balance of the Revaluation Account is the net revaluation profit or loss, transferred to the partners' capital accounts in the old ratio. For example, if a building rises by Rs 40,000 and a provision for doubtful debts of Rs 5,000 is created and creditors are overstated by Rs 3,000 (a gain), the net effect is a credit balance (gain) shared in the old ratio. With the ratio, goodwill, reserves and revaluation all settled, the partners' capital accounts are brought up to date — and the same toolkit will handle the bigger events of admission, retirement and dissolution.

examples.problem: Example 1: A building's value rises by Rs 50,000. How is this treated in the Revaluation Account?
examples.solution:
Asset up = gain.

  • An increase in an asset is a gain → credited to Revaluation.
examples.answer: Credited to the Revaluation Account (a gain of Rs 50,000).

examples.problem: Example 2: A provision for doubtful debts of Rs 4,000 is created. Treatment in Revaluation?
examples.solution:
Reduces an asset = loss.

  • Creating the provision reduces debtors (a loss) → debited to Revaluation.
examples.answer: Debited to the Revaluation Account (a loss of Rs 4,000).

examples.problem: Example 3: In which ratio is the revaluation profit or loss shared?
examples.solution:
Old ratio.

  • It arose under the old arrangement, so it is shared in the old ratio.

recap:
• Revaluation Account: asset increase / liability decrease = gain (credit); asset decrease / liability increase = loss (debit).
  • Unrecorded asset = gain (credit); unrecorded liability = loss (debit).
  • Net revaluation profit/loss → partners' capitals in the old ratio.

quiz.q: An increase in the value of an asset is ____ in the Revaluation Account.
quiz.explanation: An asset increase is a gain — credited to Revaluation.

quiz.q: Revaluation profit or loss is transferred to capitals in the:
quiz.explanation: It is shared in the old ratio.

questions.explanation: It reconstitutes the partnership.

questions.explanation: A: 3/5 − 1/2 = 1/10 sacrifice.

questions.explanation: The gainer compensates the sacrificer for goodwill.

questions.explanation: Gaining partner's capital is debited; sacrificer's credited.

questions.q: Accumulated reserves are distributed in the ____ ratio on a change in PSR.
questions.explanation: They belong to old partners in the old ratio.

questions.q: An accumulated loss (debit P&L balance) is ____ the old partners.
questions.explanation: Losses are debited to old partners in the old ratio.

questions.q: An increase in an asset is ____ in the Revaluation Account.
questions.explanation: An asset increase is a gain — credited.

questions.q: An increase in a liability is ____ in the Revaluation Account.
questions.explanation: A liability increase is a loss — debited.

questions.q: Creating a provision for doubtful debts is ____ in Revaluation.
questions.explanation: It reduces debtors — a loss, debited.

questions.q: An unrecorded asset brought into account is:
questions.explanation: An unrecorded asset is a gain — credited.

questions.q: Revaluation profit/loss is shared in the:
questions.explanation: It is shared in the old ratio.

questions.q: A, B and C share 4:3:2 and decide to share equally. C's change is:
Goodwill is Rs 90,000. A sacrifices 1/6 and B gains 1/6. The adjustment entry is:
options: B's Capital Dr 15,000; To A's Capital 15,000
A's Capital Dr 15,000; To B's Capital 15,000
questions.explanation: 90,000 × 1/6 = 15,000; the gainer B is debited and the sacrificer A credited.

questions.q: Why are accumulated reserves distributed BEFORE applying the new ratio?
options: They were earned under the old arrangement and belong to the old ratio
questions.explanation: Past reserves belong to the partners in their old ratio; only future profits use the new ratio.

questions.q: Building up Rs 60,000, plant down Rs 20,000, an unrecorded creditor Rs 5,000. The net revaluation result is a:
questions.explanation: Gain 60,000 − loss 20,000 − loss 5,000 = +35,000 profit (old ratio).

questions.q: If only the GAINING partner is to bear the goodwill and the partners agree NOT to revalue, the workmen compensation reserve (no claim) is still:
options: Distributed to all old partners in the old ratio
questions.explanation: A free reserve with no liability belongs to all old partners in the old ratio, regardless of the goodwill treatment.

questions.q: A and B (3:2) change to 2:3. Goodwill Rs 1,00,000. The single adjustment entry is:
options: B's Capital Dr 20,000; To A's Capital 20,000
A's Capital Dr 20,000; To B's Capital 20,000
questions.explanation: A sacrifices 1/5 (3/5→2/5), B gains 1/5; 1,00,000 × 1/5 = 20,000, gainer B debited.

questions.q: When assets and liabilities are NOT to be shown at revalued figures, the alternative used is:
options: A single adjustment entry through capitals (memorandum revaluation)
questions.explanation: A memorandum/adjustment approach records only the net effect through capital accounts, leaving book values unchanged.

questions.q: Total sacrifice in any change of ratio must always equal the total:
questions.explanation: What some partners give up, others take — total sacrifice = total gain.

questions.q: A debit balance of Profit & Loss Account (accumulated loss) of Rs 25,000 on a change in ratio (old 3:2) is:
questions.explanation: An accumulated loss is debited to old partners in the old ratio 3:2 → 15,000 and 10,000.

questions.q: The Revaluation Account is also known as the:
questions.explanation: It is the Profit & Loss Adjustment Account (distinct from the Realisation Account used on dissolution).
